summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court reaffirmed that counsel must be appointed at the onset of a parental rights case, but held that a later break in representation caused by the parent's own voluntary absence is not structural error so long as the proceeding remains fundamentally fair.
key_cases.relevance: It quotes and applies the statutory grounds for warrantless police protective custody and the department's assumption of temporary foster custody.
key_cases.quote: A family court must timely appoint counsel in parental rights cases.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court restated that officials must ordinarily obtain judicial authorization before removing a child and may seize a child without a warrant only on reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of serious bodily injury, though it found the exception satisfied on those facts.
key_cases.relevance: This is the circuit's en banc statement of the warrant baseline that governs Hawai'i emergency custody practice.
key_cases.quote: Under the Fourth Amendment, government officials are ordinarily required to obtain prior judicial authorization before removing a child from the custody of her parent.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that a caseworker was not entitled to qualified immunity for removing children without a court order where the record showed no articulable imminent risk of serious physical injury, and that the availability of time to obtain a warrant is irrelevant when no such risk exists.
key_cases.relevance: Generalized concern or suspicion is legally insufficient to support warrantless protective custody.
key_cases.quote: The clearly established case law requires articulable, imminent, and serious physical injury or physical abuse to children to justify removing them from their parents' home without a judicial order.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children were taken from him, and that denying him the hearing given other parents also violated equal protection.
key_cases.relevance: Emergency custody must be followed promptly by a hearing on the parent's fitness; presumed unfitness is unconstitutional.
key_cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

state_agency.name: Hawaii Department of Human Services, Child Welfare Services
state_agency.hotline: 808-832-5300 (Oahu) or toll-free 1-888-380-3088 (Hawaii Island, Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kauai), 24 hours a day, 7 days a week

mandatory_reporters: Licensed or registered professionals of the healing arts or any health-related occupation who examine, attend, treat, or provide other professional or specialized services, including but not limited to physicians (including physicians in training), psychologists, dentists, nurses, osteopathic physicians and surgeons, optometrists, chiropractors, podiatrists, pharmacists, and other health-related professionals
Employees or officers of any public or private school
Employees or officers of any public or private agency or institution, or other individuals, providing social, medical, hospital, or mental health services, including financial assistance

Employees or officers of any law enforcement agency, including but not limited to the courts, police departments, department of law enforcement, correctional institutions, and parole or probation offices
Individual providers of child care, or employees or officers of any licensed or registered child care facility, foster home, or similar institution
Employees of any public or private agency providing recreational or sports activities
Commercial film and photographic print or image processors

Members of the clergy or custodians of records therefor; a member of the clergy is not required to report information gained solely during a penitential communication, except when the clergy member believes that there exists a substantial risk that child abuse or neglect that is especially heinous, atrocious, or cruel, manifesting exceptional depravity, may occur in the reasonably foreseeable future, and a clergy member who receives reportable information from any source other than a penitential communication must report it regardless of whether the same information was also received during a penitential communication
reporting_details: Hawaii is not a universal-reporting state: only the ten categories of persons listed in Haw. Rev. Stat. § 350-1.1(a) must report, and they must report the matter immediately and orally to the Department of Human Services or the police, with a written report to follow (§ 350-1.1(c)); anyone else may report voluntarily under § 350-1.3.
